Although the patient received adequate intrapartum antibiotics and has no clinical signs of infection (normal temperature, no respiratory distress), the combination of risk factors necessitates close monitoring and consideration of antibiotic therapy per NICE NG195 guidelines.
candidate_lines.L005: The patient is categorized as INTERMEDIATE risk (Score 3) due to two contributing factors: Prolonged rupture of membranes (20.0h, >=18h threshold in this model) contributing 50% of the risk, and Elevated CRP (12.0 mg/L) contributing 50%. The absence of maternal fever, chorioamnionitis, or neonatal respiratory distress prevents classification as HIGH risk, but the elevated inflammatory marker and ROM duration exceed low-risk thresholds.
candidate_lines.L008: Prolonged rupture of membranes (20.0h) contributes 2 points (Layer 1) as it exceeds the 18-hour threshold used in this risk model, though NICE guidelines note >24h as a key risk factor for term births.

candidate_lines.L014: - Monitor urine output and fluid balance closely.

candidate_lines.L019: duration=48-72 hours pending culture results stop_criteria=Stop antibiotics if blood cultures are negative at 48 hours and the infant is clinically well, per NICE NG195 Recommendation 1.21.3 [2026 amendment].
candidate_lines.L022: Monitor vital signs (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation) every 4-6 hours. Monitor urine output hourly. Repeat CRP in 12-24 hours or if clinical status changes. Monitor for signs of respiratory distress or poor perfusion.
candidate_lines.L025: Escalate to senior neonatal team if: development of respiratory distress, temperature instability, poor perfusion, or rising CRP. Immediate escalation if blood culture positive or clinical deterioration.
candidate_lines.L028: Maintain intravenous fluids as per standard preterm neonatal protocols. Initiate or continue enteral feeding as tolerated, monitoring for feeding intolerance.

passage_catalog.S010:
Source: NICE
Section: Why the committee made the recommendations

In 2026, evidence from 3 studies showed that the risk of early-onset neonatal infection increased as the time between prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM) at term and birth increased. The 2026 committee agreed to amend the risk factor in box 1 about rupture of membranes at term to refer to the time between rupture and birth rather than prelabour rupture and onset of labour. This reflected their view that whether membranes rupture before or after onset of labour is irrelevant and that is it the overall time between rupture and birth that is important for the risk of early-onset neonatal infection. The evidence was inconclusive in identifying a specific time interval at which the risk of early-onset neonatal infection significantly increased. So, using their clinical experience, the committee decided to keep this at more than 24 hours.
passage_catalog.S011:
Source: NICE
Section: How the recommendations might affect practice

The 2026 revised wording for the risk factor for early-onset neonatal infection of rupture of membranes more than 24 hours before a term birth could increase the number of neonates requiring monitoring for early-onset infection, although current practice is already largely aligned with this so no significant change in practice or resource impact is expected. There could be an increase in the number of pregnant women, trans men and non-binary people opting for induction of labour as soon as possible after rupture of membranes rather than expectant management. The 2026 revised wording in relation to the risk of factor on maternal sepsis should ensure that suspected (or confirmed) maternal sepsis in the early postpartum period will lead to the baby being assessed for early-onset neonatal infection.
passage_catalog.S013:
Source: NICE
Section: Why the committee made the recommendations

The evidence was inconclusive in identifying a specific time interval at which the risk of early-onset neonatal infection significantly increased. So, using their clinical experience, the committee decided to keep this at more than 24 hours. In 2021, confirmed prelabour rupture of membranes without any associated timeframe was removed from box 1 because the 2021 committee decided that it was covered by other risk factors listed. The 2021 committee based their recommendations on evidence on the accuracy of clinical decision models for early-onset neonatal infection, as well as evidence on individual neonatal and maternal risk factors. As there was only limited new evidence in 2021, the framework for making antibiotic decisions after birth, involving red flags and other risk factors or clinical indicators of infection, has been retained from the 2012 guideline.
passage_catalog.S014:
Source: NICE
Section: Why the committee made the recommendation
Recommendation: rec1

Recommendation: Although the recommendations that refer to C-reactive protein (CRP) results make it clear that this measure should be used alongside factors that together help to build the full clinical picture, the 2026 committee wanted to make sure that CRP results alone were not determining antibiotic treatment. They, therefore, agreed to make a recommendation about this.
passage_catalog.S015:
Source: NICE
Section: Why the committee made the recommendation
Recommendation: rec1

Recommendation: To help with treatment decisions, the 2012 guideline on early-onset neonatal infection recommended that healthcare professionals with experience in neonatal infection should be available to provide microbiological or paediatric infection disease advice. The 2021 committee decided that this recommendation is also important when making decisions about antibiotic treatment for late-onset infection.
passage_catalog.S016:
Source: NICE
Section: Update information

May 2026: We have reviewed the evidence on the time between prelabour rupture of membranes and birth (at term) to see if this affects the risk of early-onset neonatal infection. We have also amended the risk factors related to fever and chorioamnionitis because of safety concerns. See box 1 on risk factors for early-onset infection. We have reviewed the evidence on switching from intravenous to oral antibiotics when treating suspected early-onset neonatal infection. New recommendations are marked as [2026]. See the section on switching to oral antibiotics for early-onset infection. Recommendation 1.21.3 has been amended to say 'stop antibiotics' rather than 'consider stopping antibiotics' because the committee agreed it was safe for antibiotics to be stopped if the criteria in the recommendation were met.

prompt.finding_rules: Select immutable candidate-line claim_id values, never invented text. Missing treatment/dose detail is an omission, not an unsupported affirmative assertion. Do not use medical memory or a passage absent from the actual plan evidence to claim that a missing dose was retrieved. Patient facts need not be sourced to a guideline. Distinguish a proposed treatment order from a cautious safety flag or request for expert review. Ungrounded numeric doses must actually be in the candidate; list examples. Disclose missing MA numbered citation mapping. Return empty arrays for no findings and the requested 1-5 ratings.
